books.section: Prosperity and a New World Order (1988–2000)
Reagan, H. W., Clinton, and W. (1980–2001)

options.misconception: Perot carried no state in 1992, so there were no state victories to lose in the Electoral College.
options.text: Perot won the popular vote in several states but lost those states in the Electoral College.

options.misconception: Perot appeared on the ballot in all fifty states in 1992.
options.text: Perot was barred from appearing on the ballot in most states across the country.
Each state's electoral votes go to its winner, so finishing second or third everywhere wins none.

options.misconception: The Constitution says nothing of the kind; third-party candidates can win electoral votes by carrying states.
options.text: The Constitution gives third-party candidates no electoral votes in their first national campaign for president.

rationales.A: Perot carried no state in 1992. Background: he finished second in a few states, notably Maine, but first nowhere, so there were no state victories to lose in the Electoral College.
rationales.B: Perot appeared on the ballot in all fifty states in 1992. Background: his campaign gathered the signatures to qualify everywhere, which is part of why his vote total was so large.
rationales.C:
Perot's votes were real — nearly one in five — but they were spread across states he never won. Background: the Electoral College awards each state's votes to the candidate who carries that state, so second place earns nothing.
A national fifth of the vote with no state carried means a popular-vote total with an electoral-vote total of zero.
rationales.D: The Constitution says nothing of the kind. Background: third-party candidates can win electoral votes — George Wallace won 46 in 1968 — by carrying states.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the puzzle. Nearly a fifth of the vote, zero electors — how can both be true?
2. Ask how electors are won. Background: each state's electoral votes go to the candidate who carries that state.
3. Ask where Perot finished. Second or third in state after state, first nowhere.
4. Put it together. A vote spread thin across the whole country buys no state, and no state means no electors.
Remember: the Electoral College rewards winning states, not winning a share of the national vote.

stem: Ross Perot won 18.9% of the popular vote in 1992 but no electoral votes. Which of the following best explains that result?

stimulus.source_note: Data from the American Presidency Project, via the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History.
stimulus.text:
Presidential election results, 1980–2000:

| Year | Winner | Winner's popular vote | Runner-up's popular vote | Winner's electoral votes |
| 1980 | Ronald Reagan (R) | 50.7% | Carter 41.0% | 489 |
| 1984 | Ronald Reagan (R) | 58.8% | Mondale 40.6% | 525 |
| 1988 | George H. W. Bush (R) | 53.4% | Dukakis 45.6% | 426 |
| 1992 | Bill Clinton (D) | 43.0% | Bush 37.4% | 370 |
| 1996 | Bill Clinton (D) | 49.2% | Dole 40.7% | 379 |
| 2000 | George W. Bush (R) | 47.9% | Gore 48.4% | 271 |

Ross Perot, running as an independent, won 18.9% of the popular vote in 1992 and 8.4% in 1996, winning no electoral votes in either year.
